message.content:
**Hydrogen – A Quick‑Reference Overview**

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | H‑1 (protium), H‑2 (deuterium), H‑3 (tritium) |
| | Nuclear spin | ½ (protium), 0 (deuterium), ½ (tritium) |
| | Natural abundance | Protium ≈ 99.98 %, Deuterium ≈ 0.02 %, Tritium negligible |
| **Physical Properties (STP)** | State | Gas |
| | Color | Colorless |
| | Odor | Odorless |
| | Taste | Tasteless |
| | Density | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ (≈ 1/14 of air) |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (120.95 K) |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) |
| | Specific heat (gas) | 14.304 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Molar volume | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| | Compressibility factor (Z) | ≈ 0.9 at 1 atm, 25 °C |
| **Chemical Properties** | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | First ionization energy | 13.598 eV |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV |
| | Standard enthalpy of formation (ΔH°f) | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ (by definition for elemental H₂) |
| | Standard Gibbs free energy of formation (ΔG°f) | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Oxidation states | +1 (as H⁺), –1 (as hydride H⁻) |
| | Common compounds | H₂O, H₂SO₄, HCl, NH₃, CH₄, etc. |
| | Acidic behavior | Acts as a proton donor (H⁺) in aqueous solution |
| | Basic behavior | Forms hydrides (e.g., LiH, NaH) with alkali metals |
| | Redox behavior | Strong reducing agent (e.g., in metal hydrides, hydrogenation reactions) |
| | Bonding | Diatomic H₂ (σ bond, no π bond), forms covalent bonds with many elements |
| | Hydrogen bonding | Occurs in H₂O, alcohols, amides; key to many physical properties |
| **Isotopic Variants** | Deuterium (²H) | 2.014 u, 0.02 % natural abundance, heavier, lower zero‑point energy, used in NMR, neutron moderation |
| | Tritium (³H) | 3.016 u, radioactive (β⁻ decay, t½ ≈ 12.32 y), used in fusion research, radiolabeling |
| **Nuclear Properties** | Tritium half‑life | 12.32 years (β⁻ decay to ³He) |
| | Deuterium nuclear spin | 1 (boson) – allows Bose–Einstein condensation at low temperatures |
| **Applications & Uses** | Energy carrier | Fuel cells (H₂ + O₂ → H₂O), rocket propellant (LH₂ + LOX) |
| | Industrial | Production of ammonia (Haber process), methanol, hydrogenation of fats, refining |
| | Scientific | Calibrating instruments, tracer studies, NMR spectroscopy (¹H), neutron sources |
| | Medical | PET imaging (tritium‑labeled compounds), MRI contrast agents (deuterated solvents) |
| **Safety & Handling** | Flammability | Extremely flammable; explosive limits 4–75 % (v/v) in air |
| | Toxicity | Non‑toxic as a gas; inhalation of high concentrations can displace oxygen (asphyxiation risk) |
| | Storage | Requires high‑pressure cylinders (up to 700 bar) or cryogenic tanks (liquid H₂) |
| | Environmental impact | Clean combustion (water vapor); no CO₂ emissions, but production processes can be energy‑intensive |

---

### Quick Takeaways

1. **Hydrogen is the simplest element** – one proton, one electron, and a single stable isotope (protium) that dominates natural abundance.
2. **It exists as a diatomic gas (H₂)** under normal conditions, but can form a wide variety of compounds, from acids (HCl) to hydrides (LiH).
3. **Its isotopes (deuterium and tritium)** have unique nuclear and chemical properties that make them valuable in research, medicine, and energy applications.
4. **Hydrogen’s physical properties** (low density, low boiling/melting points) make it ideal as a lightweight, clean energy carrier, but also require careful handling due to its flammability.

Feel free to ask for deeper dives into any specific property (e.g., quantum mechanical aspects, industrial processes, or safety protocols)!
